# Lecture 1

## Rationality

In lay terms, rationality inheres an actor's ability to possess *preferences*. Formally, this entails *transitivity* and *completeness*.

- \textbf{Transitivity}: Preference relations form some order of elements, whether it be weak or strong. $\forall m, n, p \in R, mRnRp \Longrightarrow mRp$
- \textbf{Completeness}: Each element is a member of a preference relation with all the other elements. $\forall m, n \in R, mRn \wedge nRm$

## Normal-form games

Normal-form games are one-shot (static) games with complete and perfect information.

$$\Gamma = (N, S, u)$$

Normal-form game notation encodes the following:

- A set of players/actors, $N = \{1, 2, ..., n\}$

  - We call any given actor of interest $i$
  - We refer to the rest of the actors, $N \backslash \{i\}$, as $-i$

- A set of strategy profiles, $S = S_1 \times S_2 \times ... \times S_n = S_i \times S_{-i}$

  - Let $m$ be the number of strategies available to each player; the building blocks of $S$ are the respective sets of the individual players' strategies, $S_i = \{s_{i1}, s_{i2}, ..., s_{im}\}$
  - $S_i$, in turn, are made up of individual strategies $\{s_{i1}, s_{i2}, ..., s_{im}\}$
  - $S$ is thus the cross-product of the set of strategies for each player
  - $S_{-i} = S_1 \times S_2 \times ... \times S_{i-1} \times S_{i+1} \times ... \times S_n$ is itself a set of strategy *profiles*, being the cross product of all the non-$i$ players' strategies

- An ordered set of utility functions, $u_i \in u = \{u_1, u_2, ..., u_n\} : S \mapsto \Re$

  - It takes in a given *strategy profile*, $s \in S$, as its input
  - It outputs a certain payoff, some number $\in \Re$

A strategy profile is the *combination of multiple* players' strategies *in a given scenario*. Broadly speaking, we will usually interact with two types of strategy profiles: the entirety of a *particular* scenario (i.e., all the players' strategies), and 'all-except-$i$'s strategies'.

**Note**: in the notation of individual strategies, the 1st subscript letter refers to the identity of the player, and the 2nd identifies a specific strategy within player $i$'s set of strategies. Additionally, we will make liberal use of dimensionality reduction using $-i$ to represent e.g., strategy profiles two-dimensionally (i.e., $s = (s_i, s_{-i})$, where $s_{-i} = (s_1, s_2, ..., s_{i - 1}, s_{i + 1}, ..., s_n)$).

\textbf{Note}: To be normal-form, a game does *not* require a dominant strategy.

### Example: prisoner's dilemma

To illustrate the above components in a bite-sized setting, take a game with two actors and two strategies each, like the prisoners' dilemma:

- $N = \{1, 2\}$
- $S = S_1 \times S_2 = \{s_{11}, s_{12}\} \times \{s_{21}, s_{22}\} = \{(s_{11},s_{21}), (s_{11}, s_{22}), (s_{12}, s_{21}),(s_{12}, s_{22})\}$
  - $s_{11} = s_{21} = \text{'confess'}$ (represented in different cases, $C$ and $c$, to aid in differentiation)
  - $s_{12} = s_{22} = \text{'defect'}$ ($D$ and $d$ respectively)
- $u_1(s_{11}, s_{21}) = -1, u_2(s_{11}, s_{21}) = -1, ...$
  - $u_1 = \begin{cases}(s_{11}, s_{21}) = -1 \\ (s_{11}, s_{22}) = 0 \\ (s_{12}, s_{21}) = -10 \\ (s_{12}, s_{22}) = -5 \end{cases}$
  - $u_2 = \begin{cases}(s_{11}, s_{21}) = -1 \\ (s_{11}, s_{22}) = 0 \\ (s_{12}, s_{21}) = -10 \\ (s_{12}, s_{22}) = -5 \end{cases}$

The utility payoffs can be represented more compactly in matrix format:

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={c,d}, left={C,D}, player names={Player 1, Player 2}, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.3, h=0.75]{-5, -5 & 0, -10\\ -10, 0 & -1, -1}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

## Solutions and strategies

### What is a solution?

A solution is a prediction of which choices rational actors in a game would make, usually culminating in some strategy profile. Such a strategy profile is called an *equilibrium*.

The most 'blunt' way to achieve equilibria in normal-form games is to pursue, whenever available, a *dominant strategy*.

### Dominant strategies

A strategy is a dominant strategy if, given you're acting *unilaterally*, you improve your own condition in every possible *scenario* by picking one particular strategy. In other words, said strategy delivers *you* a higher utility regardless of which strategy the other players pick.

Let

- $N = \{1, 2, ..., n\}$
- $m$ be the number of strategies $i$ can avail of $\therefore S_i = \{s_{i1}, s_{i2}, ... s_{im}\} \forall i \in N$

A strategy is

- *Strictly dominant* when $\forall s_{i} \in S_{i}, s_i \neq s'_i : u_i(s'_i, s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) \forall s_{-i} \in S_{-i}$
- *Weakly dominant* when **both** $\forall s_{i} \in S_{i}, s_i \neq s'_i : u_i(s'_i, s_{-i}) ≥ u_i(s_i, s_{-i})$ $\forall$ $s_{-i} \in S_{-i}$ **and** $\exists s'_i, s_{-i} : u_i(s'_i, s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i})$

### How to solve for dominant strategies

(1) Look at the payoffs for some player given some strategy of the opponent

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c c c c c} 
                              &         & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Player 2} \\
                              &         & c                                   & d                                   \\  \cline{3-4}
\multirow{2}{*}{Player 1}       & C         & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-8}, -8} & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-1},-25} \\  \cline{3-4}
                                      & D       & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-25},-1} & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-4}, -4} \\  \cline{3-4}
\end{tabular}   
\end{center}

(2) Mark the strategy that yields the higher payoff

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c c c c c} 
                              &         & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Player 2} \\
                              &         & c                                   & d                                   \\  \cline{3-4}
\multirow{2}{*}{Player 1}       & C         & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-8}, -8} & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-1},-25} \\  \cline{3-4}
                                      & D       & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{-25,-1}  & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{-4, -4}  \\  \cline{3-4}
\end{tabular}   
\end{center}

(3) A strategy that always yields the higher payoff is strictly dominant

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c c c c c} 
                              &         & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Player 2} \\
                              &         & c                                   & d                                   \\  \cline{3-4}
\multirow{2}{*}{Player 1}       & \textbf{C}        & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-8}, -8} & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{\textbf{-1},-25} \\  \cline{3-4}
                                      & D       & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{-25,-1}  & \multicolumn{1}{|c|}{-4, -4}  \\  \cline{3-4}
\end{tabular}   
\end{center}

$$u_1(s_{11}, \{s_{21}, s_{22}\}) > u_1(s_{12}, \{s_{21}, s_{22}\})$$

Since this is a symmetric game, player 2 will also choose c.

- The strategy profile $s_{\text{strict}} = (s_{11}, s_{21})$
- Therefore, the equilibrium is $u = (-8,-8)$.

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={c,d}, left={C,D}, player names={Player 1, Player 2}, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{-8, -8 & -1, -25\\ -25, -1 & -4, -4}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

### Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS)

Games to be solved by *iterated elimination* necessarily have *no* (single) dominant strategy, strict or weak. This solving technique is therefore predicated on the rational expectation that someone can be expected to 'eliminate' strictly domina*ted* choices and that the other player(s) will be able to anticipate that. To use a card game metaphor, we can anticipate a given player to rule out their worst 'hand'. A strictly dominated 'hand' does not necessarily need to be worse than both other hands.

**Note**: Iterated elimination of weakly dominated strategies may yield different results depending on the order of elimination and is thus to be avoided. Conversely, IESDS resolves to the same equilibrium regardless of order.

### How to solve by iterated elimination

(0) Choose a player to start with, e.g., the column player.

(1) Identify the highest-payoff strategy for said player given each specific strategy which may be employed by the other player (i.e., best-response strategy, see Lecture 2).

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={l,m,r}, left={U,M,D}, player names={Row, Column}, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{2,0 & 1,8 & 4,7\\ 5,2 & 2,6 & 4,3\\ 4,2 & 6,3 & 5,6}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

(2) Identify any of said (column) player's strategies with *no highest-payoff/best response* (in this instance, zero underlines) and eliminate it.

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={l,m,r}, left={U,M,D}, player names={Row, Column}, strike width=1.5pt, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{2,0 & 1,8 & 4,7\\ 5,2 & 2,6 & 4,3\\ 4,2 & 6,3 & 5,6}
  \strike<3->[1]{v}{1}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

(3) Now that we have anticipated any strategy the column player will dispose of, do the same with the row player.

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={m,r}, left={U,M,D}, player names={Row, Column}, strike width=1.5pt, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{1,8 & 4,7\\ 2,6 & 4,3\\ 6,3 & 5,6}
  \strike<2->[1]{h}{1}
  \strike<2->[1]{h}{2}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

**Note**: You can eliminate multiple 'dominated strategies' at each turn, e.g., when there is a single dominant strategy among 3+ strategies. The point is to anticipate which strategy/ies a given player will eliminate at every turn. By definition that entails *every dominated strategy* that exists for them at that given point of time.

(4) Keep rotating between players until you reach an equilibrium or you cannot eliminate anymore

\begin{center}
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={m,r}, left={D}, player names={Row, Column}, strike width=1.5pt, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{6,3 & 5,6}
  \strike<1->[1]{v}{1}
 \end{matrixgame}
 
 \begin{matrixgame}[force math, top={r}, left={D}, player names={Row, Column}, strike width=1.5pt, br]
  \payoffmatrix[w=1.5, h=0.75]{5,6}
 \end{matrixgame}
\end{center}

Your *equilibrium* $E(\Gamma) = \{(s_i, s_{-i})\}$, **not** $\{u_i, u_{-i}\}$. In this case, $E(\Gamma) = \{(D, r)\}$, **not** $\{(5, 6)\}$. The latter is instead the *set of payoffs* in that equilibrium.

# Lecture 2
## Best response strategies
### A primer on functions

The formal definition of a function $f : x \mapsto y$ is $$\forall x \in X, \exists ! y \in Y : x \mapsto y$$
Importantly, it limits the scope of 'for all $x$' to members of the set $X$, meaning that if you limit the set of domain members, there doesn't have to be a mapping 'connection' to the complete (i.e., universe) set; only the subset of the universe circumscribed by $X$ (e.g., $\sqrt{x}$ is a function $\Longleftrightarrow X = \{0, \Re^+\}$).

Injective: $\forall x_1, x_2 \in X, f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Longrightarrow x_1 = x_2$ (if the function outputs of two domain members are the same, then the two domain members are equal to each other)

Surjective: $\forall y \in Y, \exists x \in X : f(x) = y$ (every member of the co-domain is paired with at least one member of the domain)

### From best response strategy to best response function

A strategy $s′_i$ is a best response strategy of player $i$ to a strategy profile $s_{−i}$ if $u_i(s′_i, s_{−i}) ≥ u_i(s_i, s_{−i})$ for all $s_i ∈ S_i$. Put simply, it's just a way for us to describe a player's best strategy given *some strategy profile* employed by all the other players. When a best-response strategy applies $\forall s_{-i} \in S_{-i}$ (i.e., unconditional), it is a dominant strategy.

The best response function is the set-valued function $b_i : S_{−i} \mapsto S_i$ with $$b_i(s_{−i}) = \arg\max\limits_{s_i ∈ S_i} u_i(s_i, s_{−i})$$
The function $b_i$ maps the members of the domain $S_{-i}$ to the co-domain $S_i$. That is, it maps the strategies of other players to those of our player of interest. $b_i(s_{-i})$ is the function $b_i$ given the input of $s_{-i} \in S_{-i}$. In other words, the best-response function $b_i(s_{-i})$ 'takes in' a specific strategy within the set of 'other players' strategies' and outputs our player of interest's best response.

## Nash equilibrium ($E(\Gamma)$)
A Nash equilibrium is any strategy profile $(s_i, s_{-i})$ such that *when reached, no player has any incentive to deviate* because doing so will not be gainful. Formally, $$E(\Gamma) = s : s_i \in b_i(s_{-i}) \forall i \in N$$
As the Nash equilibrium is also the intersection between all players' best responses, $$E(\Gamma) = \{s_i \in b_i(s_{-i})\} \cap \{s_{-i} \in b_{-i}(s_{-i})\}$$ In other words, a Nash equilibrium occurs when $$\exists s'_i \in S_i : u_i(s'_i, s_{-i}) ≥ u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) \forall s_i \in S_i \forall i \in N$$

When $\exists ! s \in E(\Gamma)$ in IESDS, that strategy is the game's singular Nash equilibrium.

### When does a Nash equilibrium exist?
A normal form game has a pure strategy Nash equilibrium if $\forall i ∈ N$

- $S_i$ is a non-empty, convex and compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{m_i}$
- $u_i(s_i, s_{−i})$ is continuous in $s_{−i}$
- $u_i(s_i, s_{−i})$ is continuous and concave in $s_i$ (technically, quasi-concavity suffices)

Given we are mostly going to deal with one-dimensional strategy spaces $S_i$, an uninterrupted range along the number line (~ continuous, i.e., no gaps in the range) meets the criteria for convexity.

A utility function $u : S_i \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is concave if $$f(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda)y) > \lambda f(x) + (1- \lambda) f(y)$$ $\forall x, y \in S_i, x \neq y, \lambda \in [0, 1]$. We are going to encounter this again in lecture 13.

### Application: Downs' model

Downs' model of two-party competition is a theory exploring how party campaigning dynamics converge upon the pursuit of the median voter within a two-party system.

# Lecture 3
## Indifference in mixed strategies
A way to conceptualise indifference between strategies is to think of situations where you would want to be unpredictable and 'randomise' your moves, lest the other players be able to counter them.

## Drawing best response curves

# Lecture 4
## Continuous strategies
In continuous strategies, any given strategy a player chooses is picked with certainty; the pure strategies themselves are continuous. Importantly, this means that the utility functions are continuous (and twice-differentiable).

## Pareto optimality and domination
Pareto optimality is when the set of payoffs cannot be increased without sacrificing one agent's payoff. A set of payoffs within a strategy profile Pareto-dominates another strategy iff 
- $x$ is Pareto-optimal if there is no $y$ which Pareto-dominates $x$

## Solving
Solving continuous games means finding the location marking the joint maxima of all players' utility functions. Technically, the FOC/SOC are neither sufficient nor necessary conditions:
- It may return a mere local maximum, rather than the global maximum given the range of strategies
- Solving for a point that meets the criteria may take you outside of the strategy space

With that out of the way, the games you need to solve in the exam will still largely revolve around single-peaked preferences whose peak lies within the strategy space. To solve for each player's best response,

- Write all the information (players, final policy, available strategies, preferred policy, pre-bribe policy, utility function)
  - When necessary, substitute the known variables in the utility functions
- Take the derivatives of the players' utilities wrt their own strategy to find their optimal responses
- Solve for the optimal values of their respective responses

- Start from the end -> imagine you're the second firm already observing
- Whatever in the first firm's response is already given
- First firm anticipates that second firm will respond 
- Maximises their response given what they know about the other firm's response

# Lecture 5
## Dynamic games
**Dynamic games** or **extensive-form games** are games which unfold in multiple, sequential stages. We visualise them through rooted tree diagrams, with a single starting node and one or many terminal nodes.

Formally, a dynamic game $\Gamma(N, H, p, A, I, U)$ consists of

- The set $N$ of players, $i \in N$
- The set $H$ of histories, $h \in H$ (corresponds to the set of nodes), with the following important subsets:
  - The initial node, $H^0 = \emptyset$
  - Terminal histories, $H^T$
- An assignment of players to each non-terminal node, $p(h) : H \mapsto N \text{ } \forall h \in H \backslash \{H^T\}$
- An assignment of actions $p(h)$ may take to each non-terminal history (corresponds to the set of vertices), $A(h) \text{ } \forall h \in H \backslash \{H^T\}$
- Information sets, $I \subset H \backslash \{H^T\} : h, h' \in I \Longleftrightarrow p(h) = p(h')$
  - If $h, h' \in I$, player $p(h)$ is uncertain whether they are at $h$ or $h'$ (they cannot distinguish between the nodes ex ante)
  - If some information set has a cardinality of 1, $\exists I : |I| = 1$, it is a singleton
- The set of payoffs *at every terminal node*, $U = {u_i(h) : H^T \mapsto \mathbb{R}^1 \forall i \in N}$

## Actions and strategies
Unlike in static games, dynamic games inhere a distinction between action and strategy. A strategy is a plan of action for a given player in all scenarios, whereas an action is a single move (analogous to a strategy in a static game).

A strategy profile for player $i \in N$ is a correspondence $s_i(h) : H_i \mapsto A(h)$

The subgame-perfect equilibrium (SPE) or subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) is a refinement of the Nash equilibrium which removes unreasonable actions in the off-equilibrium path.

We find the Nash equilibrium in every subgame, then filter for the ones where the best responses are played in all subgames.

### Entry game

 Suppose player 2 
### "Non-credible threat"
- $(R, r)$ is not credible as a threat
  - If P1 chooses R, P1 expects P2 to respond rationally
  - Within the info set, $l$ strictly dominates $r$ and therefore $r$ cannot be part of PBE
  - $L$ weakly dominates $M$ but not $R$

## Signalling games
Signalling games broadly have two types of equilibria: separating and pooling equilibria. The implication of there being different types of equilibria is that the first player needs to be aware that even if player 1 does not know the state of the world, player 2's message may convey information to that end and result in player 2 undergoing belief updating.

### Separating equilibria
Separating equilibria are those where the messages sent by player 1 enable player 2 to distinguish between the different states of the world.

To solve for separating equilibria,

- Look for situations/strategies in which the action chosen by the two types of P1 differ
- Make an assumption of P1's action/move given its type
- Create weakly consistent beliefs for P2 and choose on sequentially rational actions by P2
- Check whether P1's actions are still the best response

### Pooling equilibria
Pooling equilibria are those where player 1 sends the same message regardless of the state of the world, resulting in an uninformative signal to player 2 and no belief updating on their part.

To solve for pooling equilibria, 

- Check for any strictly dominated strategies and eliminate them
- Start by assuming an action by P1 (same action regardless of type, since this is pooling)
- Check for which responses by P2 the action would be a mutual best response
- Calculate for which prior beliefs P2 would choose which action
  - Since P2 cannot distinguish between the different states of the world on the basis of P1's actions, the prior probability determines the action chosen by the 2nd player
- Calculate the probabilities on/off the equil path for which the assumed action by P1 would be a mutual best response
- Find a probability such that we have an equilibrium

# Lecture 9
## Cheap talk
Cheap talk games are a family of incomplete-information dynamic games where

- The first player is aware of Nature's draw, but not the second
- The payoff doesn't depend on the sender's signal

The implication of this model is that any talk is only credible if it is costly.

## Continuous Bayes' rule
### Revisiting Bayes' theorem for discrete events
Bayes' rule defines the probability of A being true given that B happened as the probability of both A and B being true divided by the probability of B, i.e., $$\Pr(A|B) = \frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr (B)}$$
We note that $$\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A) \Pr(B|A)$$
Therefore, $$\frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr (B)} = \frac{\Pr(A) \Pr(B|A)}{\Pr (B)}$$
We can also manipulate $\Pr(B)$, the probability of $B$ *unconditional of* $A$. We write it in expanded form as the probability of $B \wedge A$ *plus* the probability of $B \wedge \neg A$: 
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\Pr(B) &= \Pr(B \cap A) + \Pr(B \cap \neg A) \\
&= \Pr(A) \Pr(B|A) + \Pr(\neg A) \Pr(\neg B|A)
\end{array}$$
This means that $$\begin{array}{rl}
\frac{\Pr(A) \Pr(B|A)}{\Pr (B)} &= \frac{\Pr(A) \Pr(B|A)}{\Pr(B \cap A) + \Pr(B \cap \neg A)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(A) \Pr(B|A)}{\Pr(A) \Pr(B|A) + \Pr(\neg A) \Pr(\neg B|A)
}\end{array}$$

### From discrete to continuous
For two continuous random variables (CRVs) X & Y, Bayes' theorem is derived from the definition of the PDF $$f_{X|Y=y}(x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}$$ 
Superimposing this upon our description of the discrete Bayes' rule, we understand that the probability of $X = x$ being true given that we observe $Y = y$ is the probability of $X = x$ and $Y = y$ being true divided by the probability of $Y = y$. That is, the probability that the IV takes some value $X = x$ given that the DV takes the value $Y = y$ is equal to the probability that some observation takes values $X=x$ *and* $Y=y$, normalised by the probability of the IV being $y$.

This means that to derive Bayes' rule,

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
f_{X|Y=y}(x) &= \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)} \\
&= \frac{f_{X}(x) f_{Y|X=x}(y)}{f_Y(y)} \\
(&= \frac{f_{X}(x) f_{Y|X=x}(y)}{f_{X}(x) f_{Y|X=x}(y) + f_{X}(\neg x) f_{Y|X \neq x}(y)})
\end{array}
$$
In practice, the second form suffices, hence the brackets around the third form.

## Sequence of moves
1. Nature draws the state of the world $\omega$
2. $\omega$ is revealed to the first player, but not the second
3. The first player sends a message $\delta$
4. The second player chooses an action
5. The payoffs are realised, with the utilities being dependent exclusively on $\omega$

## Scenario: house committees in budget negotiations
The floor $F$ of a parliament must decide on a defence budget. There is an objective required level $\omega$ of spending, unknown to $F$. The defence committee $C$ knows the required spending and gives advice $\delta$ to $F$. Their incentives are partiallyaligned: whatever the required spend, the committee wants to spend just a little more. This is represented *in* $C$*'s utility function* as a bias $C > 0$.

Can there be any informative communication strategy? For that, we need to look for pure-strategy equilibria with informative messages; suppose $C$ adopting a policy of honesty such that $$\forall \omega, \delta = \omega$$

F's posterior belief is that the true state of the world is $\omega$, i.e., $$f_{X|\delta = \omega}(\omega) = \frac{f_{X}(\omega) f_{\delta|X=\omega}(\omega)}{f_\delta(\omega)} = 1$$

## Solving a cheap-talk game
- Show that there is no separating equilibrium
- Find a pooling equilibrium
  - Assume that player 1 always signals some message
  - Player 2 will therefore not undergo updating, i.e., $\Pr(\theta | \delta) = \Pr(\theta)$
  - Choose a strategy that maximises Player 2's utility since only their action determines the outcome
- Find a possible partially informative/restricted equilibrium
  - Establish condition: partially informative messaging between… which bounds?
  - Establish strategies: player 2 has a continuous strategy space, while player 1 has a finite strategy space between the different possible signals/messages
  - Find player 2's best responses to each message, given $\Pr(\theta|\delta)=\Pr(\omega\in[0,\bar{\omega}])$, and keep in mind that this is knowable to player 1
  - Find for which ranges of bias $c$ and state $\omega$ player 1 will not have any incentive to deviate
- Variation: find whether there is a partially informative equilibrium given some $c$ value (e.g., 0.1)

## Strategic information transmission
- When information transmission is costless, there is always a pooling (babbling) equilibria
- There are informative equilibria if the message is vague enough that knowledge of the messenger's biases $c$ doesn't unravel the equilibrium (more likely when $c$ is small)
- The amount of information that can be transmitted depends on how well-aligned the preferences are/how small $c$ is

Prove that if $X$ is finite and $R$ is a complete and reflexive binary relation on $X$, then $M (R,S) \neq \emptyset$ $\forall S \subset X, S \neq \emptyset$ iff $R$ is acyclic.

\textsc{First, I prove} that $M (R,S) \neq \emptyset \rightarrow R$ is acyclic by contraposition, i.e., $$\neg(R \text{ is acyclic}) \rightarrow M (R,S) = \emptyset$$

This goal is defined as $$\not \exists x \in S : xRx' \text{ } \forall x' \in S$$

I assume that $R$ is cyclic. This assumption is defined as $$x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n \rightarrow x_1 \not{R} x_n$$

with $i \in \mathbb{N}$. By implication, given $P$ is transitive, $$x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n \rightarrow x_1 P x_{i + 1}, i < (n - 1) \wedge x_1 \not{R} x_n \text{ } \therefore \text{ } x_1 \not{R} x' \forall x' \in S$$

Now, could there be any other $x \neq x_1 \in S : x \in M (R, S)$? We are left with $\{x_2, x_3, ..., x_n\}$. Given $$x_i P x_{i + 1} \rightarrow x_{i + 1} \not{R} x_i \text{ } \therefore \text{ } x_{i + 1} \notin M(R,S)$$ 

We see that $x_1 P x_2 \rightarrow x_2 \not{R} x_1$, $x_2 P x_3 \rightarrow x_3 \not{R} x_2$, etc. Therefore, no $x \neq x_1 \in S$ can be a member of the maximal set.

\textsc{Second, I prove} that $R \text{ is acyclic} \rightarrow M (R,S) \neq \emptyset$. This goal is defined as $$\exists x \in S : xRx' \text{ } \forall x' \in S$$

I assume that $R$ is acyclic. This assumption is defined as $$x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n \rightarrow x_1 R x_n$$

By transitivity and completeness of $P$, $x_1 P x_2$, $x_1 P x_3$, and so on. 

## Previous soln
\textsc{Second, I prove} that $R \text{ is acyclic} \rightarrow M (R,S) \neq \emptyset$ by contraposition, i.e., $$M (R,S) = \emptyset \rightarrow \neg(R \text{ is acyclic})$$

This goal is defined as $$x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n \rightarrow x_1 \not{R} x_n$$

I assume that $M (R,S) = \emptyset$. This assumption is defined as $$\not \exists x \in S : xRx' \text{ } \forall x' \in S$$ Recall that for $R$ to be cyclic, $x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n$ has to be true and $x_1 R x_n$ has to be false. There is nothing to be proven for $x_i, 1 < i < n$ as $x_i P x_{i + 1} \forall i < n \rightarrow x_{i + 1} \not{R} x_i$. We are left with $x_1$ and we already know that $x_1 \not{R} x' \forall x' \in S$.

Given $P$ inheres completeness and transitivity, $$\exists x_i : x_1 P x' \text{ } \forall x' \neq x_i \wedge x_1 \not{R} x_i \rightarrow \exists x_i : x_1 R x' \text{ } \forall x' \neq x_i \wedge x_1 \not{R} x_i$$ This can only be true if $x_1 \not{R} x_n$, which makes $R$ cyclic.
